query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Tailoring the in situ formation of a protective spinel oxide layer on an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy via controlled laser surface alloying can significantly enhance its tribo-corrosion resistance at elevated temperatures compared to untreated samples.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy with a conventional processing history that yields an uncontrolled, thin oxide layer under high-temperature, oxidative conditions.
generation.intervention: Application of a laser surface alloying treatment (or an engineered oxidation protocol) designed to systematically control and stabilize the formation of a dense, protective spinel oxide layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environments (approximately 700–900 °C) with simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive (oxidative) exposure, such as those encountered in extreme service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a stable, dense spinel oxide scale on the alloy surface that serves as a barrier against corrosive species and retards mechanical wear.
generation.mechanism: Controlled surface treatment promotes a robust spinel oxide that inhibits material diffusion and prevents further oxidation; this barrier reduces both corrosive attack and friction-induced wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Laser surface alloyed HEA samples will exhibit a lower wear depth, reduced friction coefficient, and slower oxidation kinetics compared to untreated HEA samples under identical high-temperature tribo-corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA samples that form a non-optimized oxide layer, leading to higher rates of wear and corrosion in extreme environments.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the approach is limited to conditions where sufficient oxygen is available to form the spinel phase and may not be applicable in environments that do not support such oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative degree of performance improvement, optimal laser processing parameters, and long-term stability of the engineered oxide layer are not yet determined and require further empirical validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA samples. One set undergoes the targeted laser surface alloying treatment to induce a controlled spinel oxide formation, while the other set remains untreated. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature conditions (e.g., 800 °C) in an oxidative and corrosive environment that imposes simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack.
measurements: Oxide layer phase and morphology characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Oxidation/corrosion kinetics measured by weight gain or electrochemical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant improvement in the treated samples (i.e., similar wear depth, friction coefficient, and corrosion rate as compared to untreated samples), then the hypothesis that engineered surface treatment improves tribo-corrosion resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Early research on HEAs has evolved from studies examining phase stability and strengthening mechanisms (e.g., ensuring single‐phase or controlled multiphase microstructures through alloying and processing routes) to investigations of high-temperature wear. In particular, the study in PMC7515071 used powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering to produce an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA, where tribological tests at elevated temperatures revealed that the in situ formation of a spinel oxide phase led to reduced wear depth and friction. Although a protective oxide appears to improve the wear resistance under high temperatures, the combined challenge of tribology and corrosion remains only partially addressed.
decision.unsolved: The open question is how to optimize and reliably control the formation of a protective surface film that simultaneously diminishes mechanical wear and resists corrosive attack in extreme high-temperature environments. The interplay between bulk alloy design and surface oxide stability has not been fully solved.
decision.lever: tailoring the in situ formation and stability of protective oxide layers (for example, via controlled surface treatments such as laser surface alloying or engineered oxidation protocols)
decision.why: This approach follows the observed trend that an HEA like AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 can form a beneficial oxide (spinel) at high temperature; by engineering the surface/interface, researchers can systematically enhance the protective characteristics, leading to superior tribo-corrosion resistance under extreme operating conditions.
